audit.sourceSummary: Read the complete 2,201-line local TeX source, from the preamble and abstract through all five sections, every theorem-like and proof environment, all displayed equations, labels and references, and the complete bibliography. The arXiv v1 PDF was additionally inspected to verify printed numbering and pagination. The source bundle contains one self-contained TeX file with no input or include dependencies. Complete attached proof environments were captured directly from the local TeX tree (9 proofs), independently of the AI explanation payload.
audit.centralQuestion: For the degenerate Eisenstein series on $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}$ induced from $\chi|\det|^s\otimes\mathbf 1$ along $P_k$, does the Fourier coefficient attached to $(3^2 1^{2n-6})$, after restriction to $\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}$, become another Eisenstein series, and what is the resulting local descent map?
audit.mainContribution: The paper unfolds the Fourier coefficient into an Eisenstein series on $\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}$ induced from $P_{k-2}$ with the same parameter $s$. It computes the unramified descended section as a normalized spherical section multiplied by three inverse local $L$-factors, establishes meromorphic local continuation, and proves conditional surjectivity at non-Archimedean places and dense image at Archimedean places at regular operator-family parameters.
verificationWarnings: Proposition 4.4 and the image assertion in Theorems 1.1 and 3.5 are conditional on operator-valued meromorphic continuation being regular at $s_0$ in fixed compact pictures. Proposition 4.2 establishes meromorphic continuation for local descended sections, but the stronger operator-family regularity is retained as an explicit hypothesis.

Remark 5.1 is an indicated application, not a completed maximal-partition theorem: the text says the cited results suggest the partition and provide a route to maximality for suitable Laurent coefficients.

External results invoked from Casselman–Shalika, Gindikin–Karpelevich, Jacquet, Dixmier–Malliavin, and the references in Remark 5.1 were identified from this paper but were not independently audited against their original publications.
The PDF has 27 printed pages. Page anchors below indicate the page on which each document unit begins.

nodes.label: Section 1
nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.statement: Introduces the degenerate Eisenstein series, the Fourier coefficient attached to $(3^2 1^{2n-6})$, the descent theorem, its unramified formula, and the proposed maximal-partition application.
nodes.role: States the problem, principal conclusions, and relation to automorphic descent.
nodes.whyItMatters: Provides the shortest overview of what is descended, where it lands, and which local properties are proved.

nodes.label: Section 2.3
nodes.title: Standing global data
nodes.statement: The paper works over a number field $F$ with adeles $\mathbb A$, fixes integers $3\leq k<n$, a Hecke character $\chi:F^\times\backslash\mathbb A^\times\to\mathbb C^\times$, and a factorizable nontrivial additive character $\psi:F\backslash\mathbb A\to\mathbb C^\times$.
nodes.role: Collects the standing hypotheses used by every global and local result.
nodes.whyItMatters: The rank change $(n,k)\mapsto(n-3,k-2)$ and all inducing representations depend on these restrictions.

nodes.label: Equation (1)
nodes.title: Degenerate Eisenstein series
nodes.statement: For a holomorphic section $f_s\in I_n(s)$ and $\Re(s)\gg0$, the series is $$E_{f_s}(g)=\sum_{\gamma\in P_k(F)\backslash\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F)}f_s(\gamma g).$$
nodes.role: Defines the global automorphic function to which descent is applied.
nodes.whyItMatters: Every global Fourier coefficient and unfolding in the paper begins with this series.

nodes.label: Equation (2)
nodes.title: The descent Fourier coefficient
nodes.statement: For the generic character $\psi_{\mathcal O}$ of $U_2(F)\backslash U_2(\mathbb A)$, the paper defines $$F_{\psi_{\mathcal O}}(E_{f_s})(g)=\int_{U_2(F)\backslash U_2(\mathbb A)}E_{f_s}(ug)\psi_{\mathcal O}(u)\,du.$$
nodes.role: Defines the global Fourier coefficient that realizes the new descent.
nodes.whyItMatters: The main theorem identifies this integral, after restriction, with another Eisenstein series.

nodes.label: Theorem 1.1
nodes.title: Introductory statement of the descent theorem
nodes.statement:
For $\Re(s)$ sufficiently large, $F_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(E_{f_s}(g))$, viewed as a function on $\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A})$, is an Eisenstein series associated to the parabolic induction

$$ I_{n-3}(s) = \operatorname{Ind}_{P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A})}^{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A})} \chi|\det|^{s}\otimes \operatorname{{\bf 1}}_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}}. $$

In addition, at a place $v$, the local descent integrals form a meromorphic family, as in Proposition the referenced result. If $\Re(s_0)\geq 0$ and this operator family is holomorphic at $s=s_0$, then the resulting local map is surjective when $v$ is non-Archimedean and has dense image in the smooth Fréchet topology when $v$ is Archimedean.
nodes.role: Introduction-level formulation of Theorem 3.5 and Proposition 4.4.
proofSketch: Unfold the Fourier coefficient and show that only one Weyl family survives.
Identify the surviving sum with an Eisenstein series whose section is a local Fourier integral.
Use local continuation and an annihilator argument to obtain the stated image properties at regular parameters.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the paper's principal global and local descent assertion.

nodes.label: Theorem 1.2
nodes.title: Introductory unramified descent formula
nodes.statement: Let $f_s=\bigotimes_v f_{s,v}$ be a factorizable holomorphic section of $I_n(s)$. At every place $v$ at which $\chi_v$, $\psi_v$, and $f_{s,v}$ are unramified, assume that \[ f_{s,v}=f^\circ_{n,v,s}, \] the normalized spherical section of $I_{n,v}(s)$. Then \[ \mathcal F_{v,s}\bigl(f^\circ_{n,v,s}\bigr) = c_v(s)f^\circ_{n-3,v,s}, \] where \[ c_v(s)= L_v^{-1}(\chi_v^2,2s+k-1) L_v^{-1}\left(\chi_v,s+n-\frac{k+1}{2}\right) L_v^{-1}\left(\chi_v,s+n-\frac{k-1}{2}\right). \]
nodes.role: Introduction-level statement of the explicit local calculation in Theorem 4.1.
proofSketch: Delete auxiliary coordinates using compact invariance and character orthogonality.
Recognize an inner standard intertwining operator and evaluate it by Gindikin–Karpelevich.
Reduce the remaining integral to a $\operatorname{GL}_3$ Jacquet integral and apply Casselman–Shalika.
nodes.whyItMatters: It identifies the exact Euler factors accumulated by the descent.

nodes.label: Section 2
nodes.title: Preliminaries
nodes.statement: Fixes the symplectic-group realization, roots and Weyl groups, embeddings, induced representations, intertwining operators, unipotent orbits, and Fourier coefficients.
nodes.role: Supplies the conventions required to parse the unfolding and local calculations.
nodes.whyItMatters: The proof is coordinate-heavy, so its embeddings and root conventions are genuine prerequisites.

nodes.label: Section 2.1
nodes.title: Symplectic groups, roots, and Weyl notation
nodes.statement: Realizes $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}$ using the anti-diagonal matrix $J_n$, identifies its Weyl group with signed permutations, and defines the root subgroups $X_\alpha(r)$ for roots $e_i-e_j$, $e_i+e_j$, and $2e_i$.
nodes.role: Provides the root-coordinate language used to classify contributing Bruhat cells and execute root exchanges.
nodes.whyItMatters: The survival conditions and every local conjugation calculation are expressed in this notation.

nodes.label: Section 2.2
nodes.title: Embeddings of the stabilizer and smaller symplectic group
nodes.statement: Defines the embeddings of $\operatorname{Sp}_2\times\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}$, the central embedding $\iota_c$, the $k$-dependent embedding $\iota_k$, and the auxiliary embedding $t_k:\operatorname{GL}_3\to\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}$.
nodes.role: Specifies how the stabilizer, descended group, and final $\operatorname{GL}_3$ Jacquet integral sit inside the ambient group.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without these embeddings, the restricted Fourier coefficient and local descent integral are ambiguous.

nodes.label: Equation (10)
nodes.title: The degenerate principal series $I_n(s)$
nodes.statement: The representation $I_n(s)$ consists of smooth right $K$-finite functions satisfying $$f(j(h_1,h_2)ug)=\chi(\det h_1)|\det h_1|^s\delta_{P_k}^{1/2}(j(h_1,h_2))f(g).$$
nodes.role: Defines the normalized parabolic induction from which the original Eisenstein series is formed.
nodes.whyItMatters: Its equivariance and modulus character produce the inducing data of the descended section.

nodes.label: Section 2.4
nodes.title: Unipotent-orbit Fourier coefficients and support
nodes.statement: Defines $V_{2,\mathcal O}$, the generic characters associated with a symplectic unipotent orbit $\mathcal O$, the corresponding Fourier coefficient of an automorphic function, and the meaning of an orbit supporting an automorphic representation.
nodes.role: Places the chosen coefficient in the general orbit-theoretic framework.
nodes.whyItMatters: Explains why the character used later is associated with the partition $(3^2 1^{2n-6})$.

nodes.label: Section 3
nodes.title: Fourier coefficients of the degenerate Eisenstein series
nodes.statement: Unfolds the global Fourier coefficient, eliminates noncontributing Bruhat families, and identifies the surviving expression with an Eisenstein series on $\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}$.
nodes.role: Contains the global geometric and combinatorial core of the descent.
nodes.whyItMatters: This section explains why the rank drops by three and the inducing block size drops by two.

nodes.label: Lemma 3.1
nodes.title: Bruhat parametrization of the double quotient
nodes.statement: We first parameterize $P_k(F) \backslash \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F) / Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(F)$ by representatives of the form $w v_w$ for $w \in W_n$ and $v_w$ in a unipotent subgroup $V_w$ depending on $w$.
nodes.proofText:
Since $U_2 \subset Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}$, we have a surjection \[ P_k(F) \backslash \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F) / U_2(F) \twoheadrightarrow P_k(F) \backslash \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F) / Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(F). \] By the Bruhat decomposition $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F) = \bigsqcup_{w \in W_n} B(F)\, w\, B(F)$ together with $B \subset P_k$, every $g \in \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F)$ admits the form $g = b_1 w b_2$ with $b_1, b_2 \in B(F)$. Absorbing $b_1$ into $P_k$ on the left and writing $b_2 = t u$ with $t \in T$, $u \in U(F)$, the relation $w t = (w t w^{-1}) w$ together with $w t w^{-1} \in T \subset P_k$ allows us to absorb $t$ as well. Hence \[ P_k(F) \backslash \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F) / U(F) = \bigsqcup_{w \in W(P_k) \backslash W_n} P_k(F)\, w\, U(F) / U(F). \]

To pass from $U$ to $U_2$, we retain the part of $U$ not in $U_2$. The decomposition $U = (U \cap M_2) \cdot U_2$ gives $U / U_2 \cong U \cap M_2 = \prod_{\alpha \in \Sigma^+(M_2)} X_\alpha$. For $\alpha \in \Sigma^+(M_2)$, conjugation gives $w X_\alpha(r) w^{-1} = X_{w \alpha}(\pm r)$. If $w \alpha \in \Sigma(P_k)$, then $X_{w \alpha} \subset P_k$, and $X_\alpha(r)$ is killed (absorbed into $P_k$ on the left after conjugation by $w$); otherwise it must be retained. Finally, since $Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}} = M_{\psi_\mathcal{O}} \ltimes U_2$, the further right quotient by $Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}$ kills those root subgroups $X_\alpha$ contained in $M_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}$ as subgroups of $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}$. The surviving root subgroups are therefore those indexed by \[ \mathcal{R}_w := \{\alpha \in \Sigma^+(M_2) : X_\alpha \not\subset M_{\psi_\mathcal{O}} \text{ and } w \alpha \notin \Sigma(P_k)\}, \] and we set $V_w := \prod_{\alpha \in \mathcal{R}_w} X_\alpha$. Every double coset in $P_k(F) \backslash \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F) / Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(F)$ admits a representative of the form $\gamma = w v_w$ with $w \in W_n$ and $v_w \in V_w(F)$.
nodes.role: Reduces the unfolding to Weyl combinatorics and explicit unipotent parameters.
proofSketch: Apply Bruhat decomposition and absorb the left Borel and right $U_2$ factors.
Retain precisely the positive-root coordinates in $U\cap M_2$ that cannot be absorbed on either side.
nodes.whyItMatters: It supplies the index set on which the subsequent vanishing argument operates.

nodes.label: Lemma 3.2
nodes.title: Necessary Weyl survival condition
nodes.statement: Among all $w$, only if $w(1),w(2)\in\{-1,\dots,-k\}$ and $w(3)\in \pm\{k+1,\dots,n\}$, the summand might contribute nonzero.
nodes.proofText:
Fix a summand corresponding to $\gamma = w v_w$. Since $\beta \in Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(F) \subset P_2(F)$ normalizes $U_2(F)$ and stabilizes $\psi_\mathcal{O}$, the change of variables $u \mapsto \beta^{-1} u \beta$ on $U_2(F) \backslash U_2(\mathbb{A})$ preserves both the Haar measure and the character, giving

$$ \int_{U_2(F) \backslash U_2(\mathbb{A})} f_s(\gamma \beta u g)\, \psi_\mathcal{O}(u)\, du = \int_{U_2(F) \backslash U_2(\mathbb{A})} f_s(\gamma u \beta g)\, \psi_\mathcal{O}(u)\, du. $$

For $i = 1, 2$, define the one-parameter subgroup $ Y_{i, v}(r) := v_w^{-1} X_{\tau_i}(r) v_w$. Then $Y_{i, v}(\mathbb{A})$ is a closed one-parameter subgroup of $U_2(\mathbb{A})$ with $Y_{i, v}(F) = Y_{i, v}(\mathbb{A}) \cap U_2(F)$, so the $U_2$-integration decomposes along $Y_{i, v}(\mathbb{A})$: \[ U_2(F) \backslash U_2(\mathbb{A}) \;\simeq\; \bigl(U_2(F)\, Y_{i, v}(\mathbb{A}) \backslash U_2(\mathbb{A})\bigr) \times (F \backslash \mathbb{A}), \qquad du = dr \, du'. \] A direct computation shows that $v_w^{-1} X_{\tau_i}(r) v_w$ differs from $X_{\tau_i}(r)$ only by root subgroups on which $\psi_\mathcal{O}$ is trivial; hence $\psi_\mathcal{O}\bigl(Y_{i, v}(r)\, u'\bigr) = \psi(r)\, \psi_\mathcal{O}(u')$. Substituting into the referenced result yields

$$ \int_{U_2(F) Y_{i, v}(\mathbb{A}) \backslash U_2(\mathbb{A})} \left( \int_{F \backslash \mathbb{A}} f_s\bigl(\gamma\, Y_{i, v}(r)\, u' \beta g\bigr)\, \psi(r)\, dr \right) \psi_\mathcal{O}(u')\, du'. $$

Using $\gamma = w v_w$ and $w X_{\tau_i}(r) w^{-1} = X_{w \tau_i}(\pm r)$, after replacing $r$ by $-r$ if necessary we obtain $f_s\bigl(\gamma\, Y_{i, v}(r)\, u' \beta g\bigr) = f_s\bigl(X_{w \tau_i}(r)\, \gamma\, u' \beta g\bigr)$. Hence the vanishing of the referenced result depends only on the Weyl element $w$ through the position of $X_{w \tau_i}$.

If \(X_{w\tau_i}\subset P_k\), then the normalized inducing character is trivial on \(X_{w\tau_i}\), since it is a unipotent root subgroup of \(P_k\), and the left $P_k(\mathbb{A})^1$-invariance of $f_s$ allows us to remove $X_{w \tau_i}(r)$ from the integrand. The inner $r$-integral reduces to $\int_{F \backslash \mathbb{A}} \psi(r)\, dr = 0$, so the summand vanishes. A necessary condition for the summand to contribute is therefore

$$ X_{w \tau_1} \not\subset P_k \quad \text{and} \quad X_{w \tau_2} \not\subset P_k. $$

In the signed permutation model for $W_n$, condition the referenced result is equivalent to the survival condition

$$ w(1), w(2) \in \{-1, \ldots, -k\}, \qquad w(3) \in \pm\{k+1, \ldots, n\}. $$

Indeed, if $w(3) \notin \pm\{k+1, \ldots, n\}$ or one of $w(1), w(2)$ lies in $\pm\{k+1, \ldots, n\}$, then $w \tau_1$ or $w \tau_2$ lies in the Levi root system of $P_k$, contradicting the referenced result.
nodes.role: Eliminates all Weyl terms incompatible with the two nontrivial root characters.
proofSketch: Decompose the $U_2$ integral along each root subgroup on which $\psi_{\mathcal O}$ is nontrivial.
If the conjugated root lies in $P_k$, left invariance makes the integrand constant along that root.
Orthogonality of the nontrivial character forces that summand to vanish.
nodes.whyItMatters: It isolates the geometric orbit responsible for the descent.

nodes.label: Lemma 3.3
nodes.title: Uniqueness of the surviving Weyl family
nodes.statement: Any other family $w' V_{w'}$ with $w'$ satisfying the referenced result is equivalent to $w V_w$ under left $W(P_k)$ and right $W(Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}})$.
nodes.proofText:
Specifically, we construct $\sigma_\ell \in W(P_k)$ and $\sigma_r \in 1 \times W_{n-3} \subset W(Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}})$ such that

$$ \sigma_\ell \cdot w V_w \cdot \sigma_r = w' V_{w'}. $$

\paragraph{Construction of $\sigma_\ell$ and $\sigma_r$.} Recall $W(P_k) \cong S_k \times W(\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)})$, where $S_k$ permutes outputs in $\{1, \ldots, k\}$ as the symmetric group and $W(\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)})$ acts on $\pm\{k+1, \ldots, n\}$ as signed permutations; the factor $W_{n-3}$ in $W(Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}})$ acts as signed permutations on $\{4, \ldots, n\}$ and fixes $\{1, 2, 3\}$.

Since $w(j), w'(j) \in \{-1, \ldots, -k\}$ for $j = 1, 2$ and $S_k$ acts transitively on ordered pairs of distinct elements of $\{-1, \ldots, -k\}$, choose $\tau \in S_k$ with $\tau(w(j)) = w'(j)$ for $j = 1, 2$. Since $w(3), w'(3) \in \pm\{k+1, \ldots, n\}$ and $W(\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)})$ acts transitively on this set, choose $\rho \in W(\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)})$ with $\rho(w(3)) = w'(3)$. Set $\sigma_\ell := (\tau, \rho) \in W(P_k)$. Then $\sigma_\ell w$ agrees with $w'$ on $\{1, 2, 3\}$, and consequently $\sigma_\ell w$ and $w'$ map $\{\pm 4, \ldots, \pm n\}$ to the same subset of $\{\pm 1, \ldots, \pm n\}$.

For $j \in \{4, \ldots, n\}$, define $\sigma_r(j) := w^{-1}\bigl(\sigma_\ell^{-1}(w'(j))\bigr)$. The argument $\sigma_\ell^{-1}(w'(j))$ lies in $w(\{\pm 4, \ldots, \pm n\})$, so $\sigma_r(j) \in \{\pm 4, \ldots, \pm n\}$ and $\sigma_r$ is a signed permutation of $\{4, \ldots, n\}$. Hence $\sigma_r \in 1 \times W_{n-3}$. Direct verification gives $w' = \sigma_\ell w \sigma_r$.

It remains to verify

$$ V_{w'} = \sigma_r^{-1} V_w \sigma_r, $$

which combined with $w' = \sigma_\ell w \sigma_r$ gives the referenced result. We establish two structural identities.

For any $\sigma \in W(P_k)$ and $w \in W_n$, $V_{\sigma w} = V_w$. Indeed, $W(P_k) = W(M_k)$ stabilizes $\Sigma(M_k)$, and applying any $(\tau, \rho) \in S_k \times W(\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)})$ to a root $e_a \pm e_b \in \Sigma(U_k)$ with $a \leq k < b$ yields $e_{\tau(a)} \pm \epsilon\, e_{\rho'(b)} \in \Sigma(U_k)$ regardless of the sign $\epsilon$, so $W(P_k)$ preserves $\Sigma(P_k)$ as a set. The condition $w \alpha \notin \Sigma(P_k)$ is therefore invariant under left-multiplication of $w$ by $\sigma$, giving $\mathcal{R}_{\sigma w} = \mathcal{R}_w$ and $V_{\sigma w} = V_w$.

For any $\sigma_r \in 1 \times W_{n-3}$ and $w \in W_n$, $V_{w \sigma_r} = \sigma_r^{-1} V_w \sigma_r$. Indeed, $\sigma_r$ fixes $e_3$ and permutes $\{e_4, \ldots, e_n\}$ as signed permutations, so it preserves $\mathcal{S}$ as a set. Then for $\beta \in \mathcal{S}$, \[ \beta \in \mathcal{R}_{w \sigma_r} \iff w \sigma_r(\beta) \notin \Sigma(P_k) \iff \sigma_r(\beta) \in \mathcal{R}_w \iff \beta \in \sigma_r^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_w), \] giving $\mathcal{R}_{w \sigma_r} = \sigma_r^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_w)$. The subgroup identity follows from the standard formula $\sigma_r^{-1} X_\alpha \sigma_r = X_{\sigma_r^{-1}(\alpha)}$: \[ \sigma_r^{-1} V_w \sigma_r = \prod_{\alpha \in \mathcal{R}_w} X_{\sigma_r^{-1}(\alpha)} = \prod_{\beta \in \sigma_r^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_w)} X_\beta = \prod_{\beta \in \mathcal{R}_{w \sigma_r}} X_\beta = V_{w \sigma_r}. \]

Combining the two identities with $w' = \sigma_\ell w \sigma_r$ we get $V_{w'} = V_{\sigma_\ell w \sigma_r} = V_{w \sigma_r} = \sigma_r^{-1} V_w \sigma_r$, which is the referenced result. Hence the referenced result holds, and $w V_w$ is a canonical representative of the unique Weyl-equivalence class of $\gamma$ that can contribute nontrivially.
nodes.role: Shows that the potentially nonzero contribution comes from one Weyl-equivalence class.
proofSketch: Use the two Weyl subgroups to match the images of indices $1,2,3$.
Construct the remaining right signed permutation on indices $4,\ldots,n$.
Check that the associated unipotent subgroup transforms compatibly.
nodes.whyItMatters: This converts a large Bruhat sum into one canonical contribution.

nodes.label: Proposition 3.4
nodes.title: Explicit unfolded Fourier coefficient
nodes.statement: Let $H=U_2^w$. Then \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal F_{\psi_{\mathcal{O}}}(E_{f_s})(g) &= \sum_{\beta' \in P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F)\backslash\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(F)} \int_{H(F)\backslash U_2(\mathbb A)} f_s\bigl(wu\iota_c(\beta')g\bigr)\psi_{\mathcal{O}}(u)\,du\\ &= \sum_{\beta' \in P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F)\backslash\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(F)} \int_{H(\mathbb A)\backslash U_2(\mathbb A)} \int_{H(F)\backslash H(\mathbb A)} f_s\bigl(whu\iota_c(\beta')g\bigr) \psi_{\mathcal{O}}(hu)\,dh\,d\dot u\\ &= \sum_{\beta' \in P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F)\backslash\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(F)} \int_{H(\mathbb A)\backslash U_2(\mathbb A)} f_s\bigl(wu\iota_c(\beta')g\bigr) \psi_{\mathcal{O}}(u)\,d\dot u. \end{aligned} \] Here we used $wH(\mathbb A)w^{-1} \subset (U\cap M_k)(\mathbb A) \subset P_k(\mathbb A)$ together with $\operatorname{vol}(H(F)\backslash H(\mathbb A))=1$.
nodes.proofText:
\newcommand{n_{2,+}^{k+1}}{n_{2,+}^{k+1}}

Fix $v=(v_1,\dots,v_{k-2})\in F^{k-2}$ and embed it in $V_w$ via the referenced result. Let $r=(r_1,\dots,r_{k-2})\in \mathbb{A}^{k-2}$. Define the $(k-1)$-tuple

$$ \bigl(\delta(r), r\bigr) := \bigl(-\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}r_iv_i,\, r_1,\, r_2,\, \dots,\, r_{k-2}\bigr) \in \mathbb{A}^{k-1}, $$

where $\delta(r) := -\sum_{i=1}^{k-2} r_i v_i$. Define $n_{2,+}^{k+1}\bigl((a_3, \dots, a_{k+1})\bigr) := \prod_{j=3}^{k+1} X_{e_2 + e_j}(a_j), $ where we have $(a_3, \dots, a_{k+1}) \in \mathbb{A}^{k-1}$.

By construction $n_{2,+}^{k+1}((\delta(r),r))\in U_2(\mathbb{A})$. Write $u=n_{2,+}^{k+1}((\delta(r),r))\,u'$ with $u'\in U_2(\mathbb{A})$. We may conjugate $n_{2,+}^{k+1}((\delta(r),r))$ to the left. The only nontrivial effect comes from conjugation by $v$: a direct computation (in the unipotent coordinates) gives

$$ v\,n_{2,+}^{k+1}((\delta(r),r))\,v^{-1}=n_{2,+}^{k+1}\!\bigl(\,\delta(r)+\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}r_i v_i,r\bigr), \qquad \delta\in \mathbb{A}, $$

so that, with $\delta=\delta(r)$ as in the referenced result, we obtain $v\,n_{2,+}^{k+1}((\delta(r),r))\,v^{-1}=n_{2,+}^{k+1}((0,r))$. Consequently, $f_s\bigl(wv\,n_{2,+}^{k+1}((\delta(r),r))\,u' \beta g\bigr) =f_s\bigl(w\,n_{2,+}^{k+1}(0,r)\,v\,u'\beta g\bigr)$.

Note that $wn_{2,+}^{k+1}(0,r)w^{-1}$ is in $P_k(\mathbb{A})$, so by the left $P_k(\mathbb{A})^1$-invariance of $f_s$, we have $f_s(wn_{2,+}^{k+1}(0,r)vu'\beta g) = f_s(wvu'\beta g)$, independent of $r$. On the other hand, $\psi_\mathcal{O}$ is nontrivial on $n_{2,+}^{k+1}((\delta(r),r))$, and by the definition of $\delta(r)$ in the referenced result we have \[ \psi_\mathcal{O}\bigl(n_{2,+}^{k+1}((\delta(r),r))\bigr) =\psi\!\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}r_i v_i\right) =\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}\psi(-r_i v_i). \] Thus, for any fixed $v\in V_w$, the Fourier coefficient contains the inner integral \[ \int_{(F\backslash\mathbb{A})^{k-2}} \left(\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}\psi(-r_i v_i)\right)\,\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}dr_i. \] By orthogonality of additive characters, this inner integral is nonzero only if $v_i=0$ for all $i=1,\dots,k-2$. Hence we may drop the summation over the discrete unipotent subgroup $V_w$. Since $Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}^w$ is independent of the choice of $v$, we obtain

$$ F_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(E_{f_s}(g)) =\int_{U_2(F)\setminus U_2(\mathbb{A})} \sum_{\beta\in Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}^w(F)\setminus Q_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(F)} f_s(w u\beta g)\,\psi_\mathcal{O}(u)\,du. $$

Furthermore, since $M^w_{\psi_{\mathcal O}}\simeq \operatorname{Sp}_2\times P_{k-2,2(n-3)}$, every class $\beta\in Q^w_{\psi_{\mathcal O}}(F)\backslash Q_{\psi_{\mathcal O}}(F)$ may be represented by a pair \[ \beta'\in P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F)\backslash \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(F), \qquad u_0\in U_2^w(F)\backslash U_2(F), \] corresponding to its Levi and unipotent components, respectively. Substitute this into the referenced result. Since $\psi_{\mathcal O}$ is trivial on $U_2^w(\mathbb{A})$ and $U_{2,w}(\mathbb{A})\simeq U_2^w(\mathbb{A})\backslash U_2(\mathbb{A})$, the summation over $U_2^w(F)\backslash U_2(F)$ can be absorbed into the integration over $U_2(F)\backslash U_2(\mathbb{A})$, giving the second line of the above. This proves the proposition.
nodes.role: Produces the precise Eisenstein-series-shaped expression.
proofSketch: Use character orthogonality to force the discrete parameter $v\in V_w(F)$ to be zero.
Identify the stabilizer intersection as $\operatorname{Sp}_2\times P_{k-2,2(n-3)}$.
Absorb the rational quotient of $U_2$ into the adelic integral and quotient by $H$.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the direct bridge from Bruhat analysis to the descended Eisenstein series.

nodes.label: Theorem 3.5
nodes.title: Main descent theorem
nodes.statement: Let $E_{f_s}(g)$ be an Eisenstein series associated with the parabolic induction $ I_n(s)=\operatorname{Ind}_{P_k(\mathbb{A})}^{\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(\mathbb{A})}\left(\chi|\det|^s\otimes \operatorname{{\bf 1}}_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)}}\right)$. For a fixed generic character $\psi_\mathcal{O}$, consider its Fourier coefficient $F_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(E_{f_s}(g))$. For $\Re(s)$ sufficiently large, as a function on $\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A})$, $F_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(E_{f_s}(g))$ is an Eisenstein series associated to the parabolic induction \[ I_{n-3}(s) = \operatorname{Ind}_{P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A})}^{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A})} \chi|\det|^{s}\otimes \operatorname{{\bf 1}}_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}}. \] The corresponding section attached to this Eisenstein series continues to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$. Furthermore, at every point \(s_0\) with \(\Re(s_0)\ge0\) at which the meromorphically continued local descent operator is regular, the local map is surjective at non-Archimedean places and has dense image at Archimedean places.
nodes.proofText:
In the initial absolute-convergence half-plane, the unfolding proved above identifies $F_{\psi_{\mathcal{O}}}(E_{f_s})$ with the Eisenstein series attached to the descended section $g\longmapsto\mathcal{F}(f_s,g)$.

Suppose that $f_s=\otimes_v'f_{s,v}$ is a factorizable standard section. Choose a finite set $S$ containing the Archimedean places and all places at which the data are ramified. For $v\notin S$, let $f_{s,v}^{\circ}$ and $f_{s,v}^{\prime\circ}$ denote the normalized source and target spherical sections. By Theorem the referenced result, \[ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v}^{\circ},g_v) =c_v(s)f_{s,v}^{\prime\circ}(g_v), \] where \[ \begin{aligned} c_v(s)={}&L_v(\chi_v^2,2s+k-1)^{-1}\\ &{}\times L_v\left(\chi_v,s+n-\frac{k+1}{2}\right)^{-1} L_v\left(\chi_v,s+n-\frac{k-1}{2}\right)^{-1}. \end{aligned} \] Consequently \[ \mathcal{F}(f_s)=C^S(s) \left(\bigotimes_{v\notin S}'f_{s,v}^{\prime\circ}\right) \otimes\left(\bigotimes_{v\in S}\mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v})\right), \] where \[ C^S(s)= \frac{1}{ L^S(\chi^2,2s+k-1) L^S\left(\chi,s+n-\frac{k+1}{2}\right) L^S\left(\chi,s+n-\frac{k-1}{2}\right)}. \] This identity first holds in the common absolute-convergence domain. Proposition the referenced result gives the required local meromorphic continuations at the finitely many places in $S$, while the preceding unramified formula gives the remaining factors. Hence the identity extends as an identity of meromorphic families. Therefore $F_{\psi_{\mathcal{O}}}(E_{f_s})$ is the Eisenstein series attached to the descended section $\mathcal{F}(f_s,\cdot)\in I_{n-3}(s)$, initially in the convergence region and then by meromorphic continuation.

At a parameter $s_0$ where the relevant operator-valued local continuations are regular, Proposition the referenced result gives exact local preimages at finite places and dense local image at Archimedean places. The general right-$K$-finite case follows locally from finite linear combinations of factorizable flat sections with holomorphic coefficients.
nodes.role: Central theorem of the paper in its definitive numbered form.
proofSketch: Use Proposition 3.4 to express the Fourier coefficient as an Eisenstein sum of descended integrals.
Verify that the descended integral transforms as a section of $I_{n-3}(s)$.
Factor the section locally and use the unramified calculation plus ramified and Archimedean continuation.
Apply Proposition 4.4 wherever the operator-valued family is regular.
nodes.whyItMatters: It proves that the Fourier coefficient preserves the inducing parameter while changing $(n,k)$ to $(n-3,k-2)$.

nodes.label: Lemma 3.6
nodes.title: The global descended section
nodes.statement:
Consider the function on $g\in \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A})$, where $g$ is embedded into the central block of $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(\mathbb{A})$, denoted by $\iota_{c}$, defined by

$$ \mathcal{F}(f_s,g) \;:=\; \int_{U_{2,w}(\mathbb{A})} f_s\!\bigl(wu\iota_c(g)\bigr)\,\psi_\mathcal{O}(u)\,du. $$

Then $\mathcal{F}(f_s,\cdot)$ defines a meromorphic section of $I_{n-3}(s)$. Moreover, if $f_s=\prod_v f_{s,v}$ is factorizable, then

$$ \mathcal{F}(f_s,g) \;=\; \prod_v \int_{U_{2,w}(F_v)} f_{s,v}\!\bigl(wu_v\iota_c(g_v)\bigr)\,\psi_{\mathcal{O},v}(u_v)\,du_v, $$

where $\psi_\mathcal{O}=\prod_v \psi_{\mathcal{O},v}$ and $g=(g_v)_v$.
nodes.proofText:
We have \[ F_{\psi_\mathcal{O}}(E_{f_s}(g)) = \sum_{\beta \in P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F)\backslash \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(F)} \mathcal{F}(f_s,\beta g), \qquad g\in \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A}). \] Thus it suffices to prove that \(\mathcal{F}(f_s,\cdot)\) satisfies the \(P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(\mathbb{A})\)-equivariance of \(I_{n-3}(s)\).

Let $P' := P_{k-2,2(n-3)}$. Take $p'=(h_1,h_2)v\in P'(\mathbb{A})$, where $(h_1,h_2)\in \operatorname{GL}_{k-2}(\mathbb{A})\times \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}(\mathbb{A}), v\in U_{P'}(\mathbb{A})$. For the Weyl element \(w\) in the above, we have $w(e_j)=e_{j-3},\text{ where } 4\leq j\leq k+1$. Hence the \(\operatorname{GL}_{k-2}\)-block of \(P'\), which under \(\iota_{c}\) acts on $\langle e_4,\ldots,e_{k+1}\rangle$, is carried by conjugation with \(w\) into the \(\operatorname{GL}_k\)-block of \(P_k\). More precisely, $w\iota_c(p')w^{-1} = p_w(p')\in P_k(\mathbb{A})$. If the Levi component of \(p_w(p')\) is written as $m_k(p')=(a(p'),b(p'))\in \operatorname{GL}_k(\mathbb{A})\times \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)}(\mathbb{A})$, then \[ a(p')=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,I_2) \quad\text{up to multiplication by unipotent factors,} \] and therefore $$ \det a(p')=\det h_1. $$ The unipotent part \(v\) is carried into the unipotent radical \(U_k\) of \(P_k\), and the \(\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}\)-factor is carried into the \(\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)}\)-factor of the Levi of \(P_k\).

We compute \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}(f_s,p'g) &= \int_{U_{2,w}(\mathbb{A})} f_s\!\bigl(wu\,\iota_{c}(p'g)\bigr)\psi_\mathcal{O}(u)\,du \\ &= \int_{U_{2,w}(\mathbb{A})} f_s\!\bigl(wu\,\iota_{c}(p')\iota_{c}(g)\bigr) \psi_\mathcal{O}(u)\,du. \end{aligned} \]

Since $w\iota_{c}(p')=p_w(p')w$, we have \[ wu\iota_{c}(p') = w\iota_{c}(p') \left(\iota_{c}(p')^{-1}u\iota_{c}(p')\right) = p_w(p')w \left(\iota_{c}(p')^{-1}u\iota_{c}(p')\right). \] Under the central embedding, \(\iota_{c}(p')\) preserves the quotient $U_{2,w}=U_2^w\backslash U_2$, and hence induces a change of variables on \(U_{2,w}\). Put $u'=\iota_{c}(p')^{-1}u\iota_{c}(p')$. The character \(\psi_\mathcal{O}\) is preserved under this change of variables. Thus, by the \(P_k(\mathbb{A})\)-equivariance of \(f_s\), \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}(f_s,p'g) &= \chi(\det h_1)|\det h_1|^s \delta_{P_k}^{1/2}(p_w(p')) \\ &\qquad\qquad\cdot \int_{U_{2,w}(\mathbb{A})} f_s(wu'\iota_{c}(g))\psi_\mathcal{O}(u')\, d\!\left(\iota_{c}(p')u'\iota_{c}(p')^{-1}\right). \end{aligned} \]

It remains to compute the Jacobian of this change of variables on \(U_{2,w}\). In the coordinates \(u(x,y,z)\) for \(U_{2,w}\), the quotient coordinate $y\in \operatorname{Mat}_{2\times(k-2)}(\mathbb{A})$ is transformed by $y\longmapsto yh_1^{-1}$.

The \(x\)- and \(z\)-coordinates undergo determinant-one affine transformations and translations preserving the character. Since \(y\) has two rows, $d(yh_1^{-1})=|\det h_1|^{-2}dy$. Thus the quotient measure transforms by $ du=|\det h_1|^{-2}du'$, and therefore \[ \mathcal{F}(f_s,p'g) = \chi(\det h_1)|\det h_1|^s \delta_{P_k}^{1/2}(p_w(p')) |\det h_1|^{-2} \mathcal{F}(f_s,g). \]

We now compare modulus characters. Since \(P_k\subset \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}\) has Levi \(\operatorname{GL}_k\times \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)}\), we have $ \delta_{P_k}(a,h)=|\det a|^{2n-k+1}$. Using the referenced result, we get $ \delta_{P_k}^{1/2}(p_w(p')) = |\det h_1|^{(2n-k+1)/2}$. On the other hand, since \(P'=P_{k-2,2(n-3)}\subset \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}\) has Levi \(\operatorname{GL}_{k-2}\times \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}\), \[ \delta_{P'}(h_1,h_2) = |\det h_1|^{2(n-3)-(k-2)+1} = |\det h_1|^{2n-k-3}. \] Thus \[ \delta_{P_k}^{1/2}(p_w(p'))|\det h_1|^{-2} = |\det h_1|^{(2n-k+1)/2-2} = |\det h_1|^{(2n-k-3)/2} = \delta_{P'}^{1/2}(h_1,h_2). \] Therefore $\mathcal{F}(f_s,p'g) = \chi(\det h_1)|\det h_1|^s \delta_{P'}^{1/2}(h_1,h_2) \mathcal{F}(f_s,g)$.

Smoothness and right \(K\)-finiteness follow from the corresponding properties of \(f_s\), and the local computations in the next section give convergence for \(\Re(s)\gg0\) and meromorphic continuation. Hence \(\mathcal{F}(f_s,\cdot)\) is a meromorphic section of \(I_{n-3}(s)\).

Finally, assume \(f_s=\prod_v f_{s,v}\) and \(\psi_\mathcal{O}=\prod_v\psi_{\mathcal{O},v}\) are factorizable. With the product Haar measure on \(U_{2,w}(\mathbb{A})\), Fubini's theorem gives the Euler factorization the referenced result in the initial domain of absolute convergence. The identity then extends meromorphically in \(s\).
nodes.role: Identifies the section underlying the descended Eisenstein series.
proofSketch: Conjugate the Levi of $P_{k-2}$ through $w$ into $P_k$.
Combine the source modulus character with the Jacobian $|\det h_1|^{-2}$ to obtain the target modulus character.
Use Fubini in the convergence region and then meromorphic continuation to obtain Euler factorization.
nodes.whyItMatters: It proves that the unfolded summand has exactly the required normalized parabolic equivariance.

nodes.label: Section 4
nodes.title: Local computations
nodes.statement: Computes the spherical local descent, proves meromorphic continuation for ramified and Archimedean sections, and studies the image of the local operator.
nodes.role: Supplies the analytic input needed to complete Theorem 3.5.
nodes.whyItMatters: The global unfolding alone does not determine the Euler factors or justify local continuation and image properties.

nodes.label: Gindikin–Karpelevich and Casselman–Shalika formulas
nodes.title: Spherical intertwining and Jacquet-integral evaluations
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem 4.1 invokes the Gindikin–Karpelevich formula for a spherical standard intertwining operator and the Casselman–Shalika formula for an unnormalized $\operatorname{GL}_3$ Jacquet integral.
nodes.role: External evaluation tools used to calculate the unramified scalar.
nodes.whyItMatters: These formulas produce the three inverse local $L$-factors in the answer.

nodes.label: Theorem 4.1
nodes.title: Unramified local descent calculation
nodes.statement:
Let $f_{s,v}$ be a spherical local holomorphic section in $I_{n,v}(s)$. The local Fourier coefficient

$$ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},g) = \int\limits_{\overline{U}_{2,w}(F_v)}f_{s,v}(u\iota(g))\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du $$

defines a local holomorphic section in

$$ I_{n-3,v}(s) = \operatorname{Ind}_{P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F_v)}^{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(F_v)} \chi_v|\det|^{s}\otimes \operatorname{{\bf 1}}_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}}. $$

In fact, we have $ \mathcal{F}_v(f^{\circ}_{n,s,v},g) $

$$= L_v^{-1}(\chi_v^2,2s+k-1)\, L_v^{-1}\!\left(\chi_v,s-\frac{k+1}{2}+n\right)\, L_v^{-1}\!\left(\chi_v,s-\frac{k-1}{2}+n\right)\, f^{\circ}_{n-3,s,v}(g). $$

where $f^\circ$ is the spherical vector in the representation space.
nodes.proofText:
It is clear that $\mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},g)$ lies in $I_{n-3,v}(s)$ by verifying the formula in the local context. Thus it remains to prove that $\mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},g)$ is holomorphic whenever $f_{s,v}$ is. For this purpose, we may assume $g=\operatorname{{\bf 1}}$.

Let $x=(x_{i,j})\in \operatorname{Mat}_{2(n-k)\times 2}(F_v)$ and embed $x$ into $\overline{U}_{2,w}$ via (the referenced result); denote the image by $\overline{u(x,0,0)}$. Equivalently, it corresponds to the roots $\{-e_i\pm e_j \mid k-1\le i\le k<j\le n\}.$ Then, for any $u\in \overline{U}_{2,w}(F_v)$, we have $\psi_{\mathcal{O},v}^{w^{-1}}(u)=\psi_v(x_{1,1}+x_{2(n-k),2})$. Similarly, write

$$ y = \begin{pmatrix} y_1\\ y_2 \end{pmatrix}\in\operatorname{Mat}_{2\times (k-2)}(F_v), \quad y_i = \begin{pmatrix} y_{i,1}&y_{i,2}&\cdots&y_{i,(k-2)} \end{pmatrix},\; i =1,2, $$

and denote its embedding in $\overline{U}_{2,w}$ by $\overline{u(0,y,0)}$.

Since $f_{s,v}$ is spherical and locally constant, for any $y$ such that $y_{i,j}\in \mathcal{O}_v$ for $i=1,2$ and $j=1,\dots,k-2$, we have

$$ f_{s,v}(\overline{u(0,y,0)}) = f_{s,v}(\operatorname{{\bf 1}}). $$

Now consider any $(k-2)$-tuple $r=(r_1,\dots,r_{k-2})\in (\mathcal{O}_v)^{k-2}$ and define

$$ n_{+,\,k+1}^{\,k-2}(r) \;:=\; \prod_{i=1}^{k-2} X_{e_i+e_{k+1}}(r_i)\ \in \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F_v), $$

where the product is taken in any fixed order. Note that $f_{s,v}$ is left-invariant under $n_{+,\,k+1}^{\,k-2}(r)$ since $n_{+,\,k+1}^{\,k-2}(r)\in U_k(F_v)$. Moreover,

$$ n_{+,\,k+1}^{\,k-2}(r)\begin{pmatrix} I_{k-2}&&&&\\ &I_2&&&\\ 0&x&I_{2(n-k)}&&\\ y&z&x^\ast&I_2&\\ 0&y^\ast&0&&I_{k-2}\end{pmatrix}(n_{+,\,k+1}^{\,k-2}(r))^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} I_{k-2}&b&&&\\ &I_2&&&\\ 0&x'&I_{2(n-k)}&&\\ y&z&(x')^\ast&I_2&b^\ast\\ 0&y^\ast&0&&I_{k-2}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $x$ is viewed in the form $\operatorname{Mat}_{2(n-k)\times 2}$ and

$$ x' = \begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1}+\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}y_{2,i}r_i&x_{1,2} +\sum_{i=1}^{k-2} y_{1,i}r_i\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ x_{2(n-k),1}&x_{2(n-k),2} \end{pmatrix}. $$

Before integrating over the \(y\)-coordinates, write \(y=(y_1,y_2)\) and define the partial integral \[ G(y_1,y_2) = \int f_{s,v}(u(x,y,z)) \psi_v(x_{1,1}+x_{2(n-k),2})\,dx\,dz , \] where the integration is over all remaining \(x\)- and \(z\)-coordinates in \(\overline U_{2,w}(F_v)\). Thus \[ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},\operatorname{{\bf 1}})=\int G(y_1,y_2)\,dy_1\,dy_2 . \]

On the right-hand side of the referenced result, the entries \(b\) and \(b^\ast\) lie in the unipotent radical of the \(\operatorname{GL}_k\)-Levi block inside \(P_k(F_v)\). Hence their left action on the section is trivial by \(P_k\)-equivariance. Conjugating \(n_{+,\,k+1}^{\,k-2}(r)\) to the right, using right \(K_v\)-invariance of the spherical section, and then making the changes of variables \[ x_{1,1}\mapsto x_{1,1}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}y_{2,i}r_i,\qquad x_{1,2}\mapsto x_{1,2}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}y_{1,i}r_i, \] we obtain, for every \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_{k-2})\in\mathcal{O}_v^{k-2}\), \[ G(y_1,y_2) = \psi_v\!\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}y_{2,i}r_i\right)G(y_1,y_2). \] Since \(\psi_v\) has conductor \(\mathcal{O}_v\), this identity forces $G(y_1,y_2)=0 $ unless $y_2\in\mathcal{O}_v^{k-2}$.

Indeed, if some \(y_{2,i}\notin\mathcal{O}_v\), one can choose \(r_i\in\mathcal{O}_v\) so that \(\psi_v(-y_{2,i}r_i)\neq 1\). On the remaining set \(y_2\in\mathcal{O}_v^{k-2}\), the corresponding unipotent element belongs to \(K_v\). By the referenced result, the right-invariance by compact subgroup, and normalization of Haar measure, the integration over \(y_2\) contributes volume \(1\) and may be omitted.

Similarly, considering

$$ \begin{pmatrix} I_{k-2}&0&^tr&&&&\\ 0&I_2&0&&&&\\ 0&0&1&&&&\\ &&&I_{2(n-k-1)}&&&\\ &&&&1&0&r^\ast\\ &&&&0&I_2&0\\ &&&&0&0&I_{k-2} \end{pmatrix} $$

and repeating the same argument, we can drop the integration over $y_1$ as well. Consequently, (the referenced result) reduces to

$$ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},\operatorname{{\bf 1}}) = \int\limits_{\overline{U}^{(0)}_{2,w}(F_v)} f_{s,v}(u)\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du, $$

where $\overline{U}^{(0)}_{2,w}$ has elements $\overline{u(x,0,z)}\in \overline{U}_{2,w}$. Define \[ \overline U'_{2,w} = \left\{ u(x,0,z)\;\middle|\; x= \begin{pmatrix} 0&x_{1,2}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ 0&x_{2(n-k),2} \end{pmatrix}, \quad z= \begin{pmatrix} 0&z_3\\ 0&0 \end{pmatrix} \right\}, \] and \[ \overline U''_{2,w} = \left\{ u(x,0,z)\;\middle|\; x= \begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1}&0\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ x_{2(n-k),1}&0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad z= \begin{pmatrix} z_1&0\\ z_2&z_1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}. \] Then $\overline{U}^{(0)}_{2,w}\simeq \overline{U}'_{2,w}\ltimes \overline{U}''_{2,w}$, and hence

$$ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},\operatorname{{\bf 1}}) = \int\limits_{\overline{U}''_{2,w}(F_v)}\int\limits_{\overline{U}'_{2,w}(F_v)} f_{s,v}(u'u'')\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u'u'')\,du'\,du''. $$

For $u\in \overline{U}'_{2,w}(F_v)$, write $u=\overline{u(X',0,Z')}$ where \[X'=\begin{pmatrix} 0&r_1\\ 0&r_2\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ 0&r_{2(n-k)} \end{pmatrix}, Z'=\begin{pmatrix} 0&m+\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n-k}r_ir_{2(n-k)+1-i}\\0&0 \end{pmatrix}.\] Thus $u$ can now be parametrized by $u_{(r_1,r_2,\cdots,r_{2(n-k)};m)}$.

Consider the following set of roots \[ \mathcal R = \{ -e_k+e_j: k+1\le j\le n\} \cup \{-2e_k\} \cup \{ -e_k-e_j: k+2\le j\le n\}. \] Let $N_{\mathcal R}(F_v):=\prod_{\alpha\in\mathcal R}X_\alpha(F_v)$, where the product is taken in the ordering compatible with the coordinates $(r_1,\ldots,r_{2(n-k)-1})$ appearing in $u_{(r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_{2(n-k)-1},0;m)}$. Hence we may write \[ u_{(r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_{2(n-k)-1},0;m)} = n_{\mathcal R}u', \qquad n_{\mathcal R}\in N_{\mathcal R}(F_v), \quad u'\in X_{-e_k-e_{k+1}}(F_v). \]

Define \[ w_0 = s_{k+1}s_{k+2}\cdots s_{n-1}s_n s_{n-1}\cdots s_{k+1}s_k. \] Therefore $w_0$ takes $k$ to $-(k+1)$, and takes $k+1$ to $k$ and so $w_0(\mathcal R)\subset \Sigma^+$. On the other hand, $w_0(-e_k-e_{k+1})=e_{k+1}-e_k\in\Sigma^-$. Thus \(w_0\) sends precisely the root subgroups in \(N_{\mathcal R}\) to positive root subgroups, while the remaining subgroup \(X_{-e_k-e_{k+1}}\) is not included in this intertwining step. In this common region of absolute convergence, we may separate the \(N_{\mathcal R}(F_v)\)-coordinates by Fubini's theorem. Moreover, \[ \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(n_{\mathcal R}u'u'') = \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u'u'') \] for \(n_{\mathcal R}\in N_{\mathcal R}(F_v)\), \(u'\in X_{-e_k-e_{k+1}}(F_v)\), and \(u''\in \overline U''_{2,w}(F_v)\). Hence \((the referenced result)\) becomes

$$ \int\limits_{\overline{U}''_{2,w}(F_v)} \int\limits_{X_{-e_k-e_{k+1}}(F_v)} \int\limits_{N_{\mathcal R}(F_v)} f_{s,v}(n_{\mathcal R}u'u'')\, \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u'u'')\, dn_{\mathcal R}\,du'\,du''. $$

Since $\mathcal R=\{\alpha\in\Sigma^-:w_0\alpha\in\Sigma^+\}$, the inner integration over \(N_{\mathcal R}(F_v)\) is precisely the standard local intertwining integral attached to the single Weyl element \(w_0\). Thus it defines $M(w_0,s): I_n(\Lambda_{s,v}) \longrightarrow I_n(\Lambda_{s,v}^{w_0})$. Hence the identity obtained in the above region of absolute convergence extends meromorphically.

We now check that the standard intertwining operator is defined and absolutely convergent in a right half-plane. For a positive root \(\beta\) satisfying \(w_0^{-1}\beta\in\Sigma^-\), the corresponding rank-one integral is absolutely convergent provided $\left|\Lambda_{s,v}(\beta^\vee(\varpi))\right|<1$. Write $a=s+\frac{k-1}{2}$. The positive roots \(\beta\) satisfying \(w_0^{-1}\beta\in\Sigma^-\) are \[ \{e_k-e_j:k+1\le j\le n\} \cup \{2e_k\} \cup \{e_k+e_j:k+2\le j\le n\}. \] For these roots, using the definition of \(\Lambda_{s,v}\), we have \[ \Lambda_{s,v}((e_k-e_j)^\vee(\varpi)) = \chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(a+n-j+1)} \qquad(k+1\le j\le n), \] \[ \Lambda_{s,v}((2e_k)^\vee(\varpi)) = \chi_v(\varpi)q^{-a}, \] and $\Lambda_{s,v}((e_k+e_j)^\vee(\varpi)) = \chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(a+j-n-1)} (k+2\le j\le n)$. Since \(\chi_v\) is unitary, the convergence conditions are $\Re(a+n-j+1)>0\text{ where }(k+1\le j\le n)$, $\Re(a)>0$, and $\Re(a+j-n-1)>0\text{ where }(k+2\le j\le n)$. The strongest of these inequalities is $\Re(a+k-n+1)>0$.

Therefore, after enlarging the right half-plane if necessary, the standard intertwining integral defining \(M(w_0,s)\) is absolutely convergent. The identity obtained in this region then extends meromorphically in \(s\) by the standard meromorphic continuation of local intertwining operators.

Let \(f^{w_0}_{s,v}\) be the normalized spherical vector in \(I_n(\Lambda_{s,v}^{w_0})\). By the Gindikin--Karpelevich formula for the single Weyl element \(w_0\), we have $M(w_0,s)f_{s,v} = c(w_0,s)f^{w_0}_{s,v}$, where \[ c(w_0,s) = \prod_{\substack{\beta\in\Sigma^+\\ w_0^{-1}\beta\in\Sigma^-}} \frac{ 1-q^{-1}\Lambda_{s,v}(\beta^\vee(\varpi)) }{ 1-\Lambda_{s,v}(\beta^\vee(\varpi)) }. \] In the present case, the positive roots \(\beta\) satisfying \(w_0^{-1}\beta\in\Sigma^-\) are \[ \{e_k-e_j:k+1\le j\le n\} \cup \{2e_k\} \cup \{e_k+e_j:k+2\le j\le n\}. \] Equivalently, the negatives of these roots are precisely the roots in \(\mathcal R\). Evaluating the inducing character \(\Lambda_{s,v}\) on the corresponding coroots gives \[ c(w_0,s) = \frac{ 1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-\left(s+\frac{k-1}{2}-k+n+1\right)} }{ 1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-\left(s+\frac{k-1}{2}+k-n+1\right)} }. \] Therefore \((the referenced result)\) equals

$$ \frac{ 1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-\left(s+\frac{k-1}{2}-k+n+1\right)} }{ 1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-\left(s+\frac{k-1}{2}+k-n+1\right)} } \int\limits_{\overline{U}^{+}_{2,w}(F_v)} f^{w_0}_{s,v}(w_0u)\, \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du, $$

where

$$ \overline{U}^{+}_{2,w} = \left\{\left.\begin{pmatrix} I_{k-2}&&&&\\ &I_2&&&\\ 0&x&I_{2(n-k)}&&\\ 0&z&x^\ast&I_2&\\ 0&0&0&&I_{k-2} \end{pmatrix}\right\vert x = \begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1}&0\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ x_{2(n-k)-1,1}&0\\ x_{2(n-k),1}&x_{2(n-k),2} \end{pmatrix},\; z= \begin{pmatrix} z_1'&0\\z_2&z_1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}, $$

where $z_1'$ is $z_1+x_{1,1}x_{2(n-k),2}$.

We parameterize any $u\in \overline{U}^{+}_{2,w}$ by $u=u_{(x_{2(n-k),2};x_{1,1},\cdots,x_{2(n-k),1};c_1,c_2)}$ via $\overline{u(X',0,Z')}$ where \[ X'=\begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1}&0\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ x_{2(n-k)-1,1}&0\\ x_{2(n-k),1}&x_{2(n-k),2} \end{pmatrix},\quad Z'=\begin{pmatrix} c_1+x_{1,1}x_{2(n-k),2}&0\\ c_2 + \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n-k}x_{i,1} x_{2(n-k)+1-i,1}&c_1+x_{1,1}x_{2(n-k),2} \end{pmatrix}. \] As before, if $x_{i,1},c_2\in \mathcal{O}_v$ for all $i=2,\dots,2(n-k)$, then $f_{s,v}^{w_0}(w_0u)=f_{s,v}^{w_0}(w_0)$, for all $u=u_{(0;0,x_{2,1},\dots,x_{2(n-k),1};0,c_2)}$.

Let $(r,m;t):=(r_2,\dots,r_{2(n-k)-1};\,m;\,t)\in (\mathcal{O}_v)^{2(n-k)}$. For $j=k+2,\dots,n$ set $a_j:=r_{j-k}\text{ and } b_j:=r_{\,2n-j-k+1}$. Define

$$ \begin{aligned} n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t) :=\;& X_{e_{k-1}-e_k}(t)\, \Bigl(\prod_{j=k+2}^{n} X_{e_{k-1}-e_j}(a_j)\Bigr)\, X_{2e_{k-1}}(m)\\ &\times \Bigl(\prod_{j=k+2}^{n} X_{e_{k-1}+e_j}(b_j)\Bigr)\, X_{e_{k-1}+e_k}(t) \ \in \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F_v). \end{aligned} $$

With this ordering, the long-root coordinate in the central factor becomes \[ m_r \;=\; m+\sum_{j=k+2}^{n} a_j b_j +t^2 \;=\; m+\sum_{i=2}^{n-k} r_i\,r_{2(n-k)+1-i}+t^2, \] by the commutator relations for the pairs $\bigl(e_{k-1}-e_j,\;e_{k-1}+e_j\bigr)$. Clearly $f^{w_0}_{s,v}$ is left-invariant under $n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)$. Conjugating by $w_0$ to the right, we have

$$ n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)^{w_0} := w_0n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)w_0^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} I_{k-2}&&&&&&&&\\ &1&&&&t&&&\\ &&1&0&0&0&0&&\\ &&&1&r&m_r&0&t&\\ &&&&I_{2(n-k-1)}&r^\ast&0&&\\ &&&&&1&0&&\\ &&&&&&1&&\\ &&&&&&&1&\\ &&&&&&&&I_{k-2}\\ \end{pmatrix}. $$

Conjugating $u$ by $n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)^{w_0}$ gives

$$ \begin{split} u^{\left(n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)^{w_0}\right)} = \begin{pmatrix} I_{k-2}&&&&\\ &I_2&&&\\ 0&X'&I_{2(n-k)}&&\\ 0&Z'&X'^\ast&I_2&\\ 0&0&0&&I_{k-2}\end{pmatrix},\text{ where }\\ X'=\begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1} + \sum\limits_{i=2}^{2(n-k)-1}x_{i,1}r_i + x_{2(n-k),1}m+ c_2t&x_{2(n-k),2}m\\ x_{2,1}&x_{2(n-k),2}r_{2(n-k)-1}\\ \vdots & \vdots\\ x_{2(n-k)-1,1}&x_{2(n-k),2}r_2\\ x_{2(n-k),1}&x_{2(n-k),2} \end{pmatrix}. \end{split} $$

We do not list the entries of \(Z'\), since the character \(\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}\) does not depend on them. The entries in the second column of \(X'\), except for the last entry \(x_{2(n-k),2}\), correspond to root subgroups whose roots lie in \(\mathcal R\). Since \(w_0(\mathcal R)\subset \Sigma^+\), these root subgroups are conjugated by \(w_0\) into the positive unipotent subgroup. Hence their contribution appears on the left of \(w_0\), where it is killed by the left unipotent invariance of the induced section. Thus we may replace $X'$ in (the referenced result) by \[ X'= \begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1} + \sum\limits_{i=2}^{2(n-k)-1}x_{i,1}r_i + x_{2(n-k),1}m+ c_2t&0\\ x_{2,1}&0\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ x_{2(n-k)-1,1}&0\\ x_{2(n-k),1}&x_{2(n-k),2} \end{pmatrix}, \] so that $u^{n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)^{w_0}}\in \overline{U}^{+}_{2,w}(F_v)$ and $f_{s,v}^{w_0}(n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)w_0u) = f_{s,v}^{w_0}(w_0u^{(n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)^{w_0})})$.

We now apply the same character-orthogonality argument before integrating over the coordinates which will be deleted. Put $\mathbf x=(x_{2,1},\ldots,x_{2(n-k),1},c_2)$ and define the partial integral \[ H(\mathbf x)= \int f^{w_0}_{s,v}(w_0u)\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{rem}}, \] where the integration is over all coordinates of \(\overline U^+_{2,w}(F_v)\) except \(x_{2,1},\ldots,x_{2(n-k),1}\) and \(c_2\). Thus $\int_{\overline U^+_{2,w}(F_v)} f^{w_0}_{s,v}(w_0u)\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du = \int H(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x$.

By the preceding conjugation formula, for \(r_i,m,t\in\mathcal{O}_v\), conjugation by \(n_{\mathrm{H}}(r,m;t)^{w_0}\), followed by right \(K_v\)-invariance of the spherical section, changes the character-relevant coordinate by $x_{1,1} \mapsto x_{1,1} +\sum_{i=2}^{2(n-k)-1}x_{i,1}r_i +x_{2(n-k),1}m +c_2t$. Equivalently, by change of variables $x_{1,1}\mapsto x_{1,1} -\left( \sum_{i=2}^{2(n-k)-1}x_{i,1}r_i +x_{2(n-k),1}m +c_2t \right)$, we obtain \[ H(\mathbf x) = \psi_v\!\left( -\sum_{i=2}^{2(n-k)-1}x_{i,1}r_i -x_{2(n-k),1}m -c_2t \right)H(\mathbf x). \] Since \(r_i,m,t\) range independently over \(\mathcal{O}_v\), and since \(\psi_v\) has conductor \(\mathcal{O}_v\), this forces $H(\mathbf x)=0$ unless $x_{i,1}\in\mathcal{O}_v$ where $2\le i\le 2(n-k), c_2\in\mathcal{O}_v$.

On this compact set, the corresponding unipotent elements lie in \(K_v\). By right \(K_v\)-invariance of the spherical section and our normalization \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal{O}_v)=1\), the integrations over these coordinates may be omitted. Therefore

$$ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},\operatorname{{\bf 1}}) = \frac{1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s+\frac{k-1}{2}-k+n+1)}}{1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s+\frac{k-1}{2}+k-n+1)}} \int\limits_{\overline{U}^{-}_{2,w}(F_v)} f^{w_0}_{s,v}(w_0u) \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du . $$

where

$$ \overline{U}^{-}_{2,w} = \left\{\left.\begin{pmatrix} I_{k-2}&&&&\\ &I_2&&&\\ 0&x&I_{2(n-k)}&&\\ 0&z&x^\ast&I_2&\\ 0&0&0&&I_{k-2} \end{pmatrix}\right\vert x = \begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1}&0\\ 0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0\\ 0&x_{2(n-k),2} \end{pmatrix},\; z= \begin{pmatrix} z_1'&0\\0&z_1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}, $$

where $z_1'=z_1+x_{1,1}x_{2(n-k),2}$.

Embed \(h\in \operatorname{GL}_3(F_v)\) into \(\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F_v)\) via \(t(h)\), as defined in the referenced result, and denote by \(U_{\operatorname{GL}_3}\) the embedded image of the unipotent radical of the standard Borel subgroup \(B_{\operatorname{GL}_3}\). We identify \(\overline{U}^{-}_{2,w}(F_v)\) with \(U_{\operatorname{GL}_3}(F_v)\) as follows: for \(u\in \overline{U}^{-}_{2,w}(F_v)\) in the form the referenced result, we can write \[ u = w_0^{-1} (w^k)^{-1} \, t\!\left(\begin{pmatrix} 1&x_{2(n-k),2}&z_1 + x_{1,1}x_{2(n-k),2}\\ &1&x_{1,1}\\ &&1 \end{pmatrix}\right) \, w^kw_0, \] where $w^k=w_kw_{k-1}w_k = t\!\left(\begin{pmatrix} &&1\\ &1&\\ 1&& \end{pmatrix}\right)$. Under this identification, $\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)=\psi_v(x_{1,1}+x_{2(n-k),2})$, which is the Gelfand--Graev character on \(U_{\operatorname{GL}_3}(F_v)\). Hence the integral in the referenced result is the unnormalized Jacquet integral attached to the spherical section of the unramified principal series \[ \operatorname{Ind}_{B_{\operatorname{GL}_3}(F_v)}^{\operatorname{GL}_3(F_v)} \left(\chi_v|\cdot|^{s+\frac{k-3}{2}}\otimes |\cdot|^{k-n}\otimes \chi_v^{-1}|\cdot|^{-s-\frac{k-1}{2}}\right). \]

The Casselman--Shalika formula [[cite:CS80]] applies to this unnormalized Jacquet integral and gives

$$ \begin{split} &\frac{1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s+\frac{k-1}{2}-k+n+1)}}{1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s+\frac{k-1}{2}+k-n+1)}} \int\limits_{U_{\operatorname{GL}_3}(F_v)} f^{w_0}_{s,v}\left(t\!\left(\begin{pmatrix} &&1\\ &1&\\ 1&& \end{pmatrix}\right)uw^kw_0\right) \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du\\ &= \left(1-\chi_v^2(\varpi)q^{-(2s+k-1)}\right) \left(1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s+\frac{k-1}{2}-k+n)}\right) \left(1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s+\frac{k-1}{2}+k-n+1)}\right)\\ &\quad\times \frac{1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s+\frac{k-1}{2}-k+n+1)}}{1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s+\frac{k-1}{2}+k-n+1)}} f_{s,v}(w^kw_0)\\ &= \left(1-\chi_v^2(\varpi)q^{-(2s+k-1)}\right) \left(1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s-\frac{k+1}{2}+n)}\right) \left(1-\chi_v(\varpi)q^{-(s-\frac{k-1}{2}+n)}\right) f_{s,v}(\operatorname{{\bf 1}}). \end{split} $$

In the last step we used that \(w^kw_0\in K_v\), hence the spherical section satisfies \(f_{s,v}(w^kw_0)=f_{s,v}(\operatorname{{\bf 1}})\). This proves the stated formula and completes the proof.
nodes.role: Determines the unramified local normalization of the descent.
proofSketch: Use root conjugations and character orthogonality to delete the $y$-coordinates.
Extract a standard intertwining integral corresponding to a Weyl element $w_0$ and evaluate its spherical scalar.
Delete further compact coordinates by a Heisenberg-type conjugation argument.
Identify the remaining integral with a generic $\operatorname{GL}_3$ Jacquet integral and apply Casselman–Shalika.
nodes.whyItMatters: It makes the descended global section Eulerian and explicitly records its unramified correction factors.

citations.title: The unramified principal series of $p$-adic groups. {II.} {The} {Whittaker} function.
citations.text: W. Casselman and J. Shalika. The unramified principal series of $p$-adic groups. {II.} {The} {Whittaker} function. Compositio Mathematica, 41(2):207--231, 1980.

nodes.label: Proposition 4.2
nodes.title: Ramified and Archimedean meromorphic continuation
nodes.statement:
Let $f_{s,v}\in I_{n,v}(s)$ be a section that varies holomorphically in $s\in\mathbb{C}$. Then the local Fourier coefficient

$$ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},g) = \int\limits_{\overline{U}_{2,w}(F_v)}f_{s,v}\bigl(u\iota(g)\bigr)\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du $$

defines a local meromorphic section in

$$ I_{n-3,v}(s) = \operatorname{Ind}_{P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F_v)}^{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(F_v)} \chi_v|\det|^{s}\otimes \operatorname{{\bf 1}}_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}}. $$
nodes.proofText:
We have the \(P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F_v)\)-equivariance of \(\mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},\cdot)\), hence it remains to justify convergence for \(\Re(s)\gg0\) and meromorphic continuation of the local integral. Also, since \[ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},g) = \mathcal{F}_v\bigl(\rho(\iota(g))f_{s,v},1\bigr),\] and right translation preserves smooth holomorphic sections, it is enough to consider the value at \(g=1\).

Let us first assume that \(v\) is non-Archimedean. We write \(\overline U_{2,w}(F_v)\) as in the referenced result. Thus the coordinates contain the block \[ y=\binom{y_1}{y_2}\in \operatorname{Mat}_{2\times(k-2)}(F_v), \qquad y_1,y_2\in F_v^{k-2}. \] Denote by \(\overline U^{(0)}_{2,w}\) the subgroup obtained by setting these \(y\)-coordinates equal to zero.

We first ``remove'' the \(y_2\)-coordinates. Let \[ n(r)=n_{+,\,k+1}^{\,k-2}(r),\qquad r=(r_1,\ldots,r_{k-2})\in F_v^{k-2}, \] be the corresponding product of root subgroups in \(U_k(F_v)\), as in the unramified computation. Since \(f_{s,v}\) is smooth, there exists a compact open subgroup \(K_f\subset \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F_v)\) such that $f_{s,v}(g\kappa)=f_{s,v}(g),\kappa\in K_f$. Choose \(N\geq 0\) sufficiently large so that $n(r)\in K_f \text{ for all }r\in \varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}$, and also such that the \(y\)-root elements \(u(0,y,0)\) lie in \(K_f\) whenever all coordinates of \(y\) lie in \(\varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v\).

The calculation from the unramified case gives, for \(r\in \varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}\), \[ n(r)\,u(x,y,z)\,n(r)^{-1}=b(r,x,y,z)u(x',y,z), \] where \(b(r,x,y,z)\) lies in the unipotent radical of the inducing parabolic and hence does not affect the section, and where the relevant change in the \(x\)-coordinates is $x'_{1,1}=x_{1,1}+\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}y_{2,i}r_i$.

The remaining changes in the coordinates are irrelevant for the character or are absorbed by a measure-preserving change of variables. Since \(n(r)\in K_f\), right \(K_f\)-invariance and left \(U_k(F_v)\)-invariance imply that the inner integral, viewed as a function of \(y_2\), satisfies \[ G(y_2) = \psi_v\!\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}y_{2,i}r_i\right)G(y_2) \qquad \left(r\in\varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}\right). \] Therefore \(G(y_2)=0\) unless $\psi_v\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}y_{2,i}r_i\right)=1 \text{ for all } r\in\varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}$. Equivalently, $y_2\in \left(\varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}\right)^\vee$. If the conductor of \(\psi_v\) is \(\mathfrak d_{\psi_v}\), this dual lattice is of the form $\left(\varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v\right)^\vee = \varpi^{-N}\mathfrak d_{\psi_v}^{-1}\mathcal{O}_v = \varpi^{-M}\mathcal{O}_v$ for some integer \(M\). Thus the \(y_2\)-integration is supported in the compact lattice \(\varpi^{-M}\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}\).

Now decompose this lattice into finitely many cosets modulo \(\varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}\): \[ \varpi^{-M}{\mathcal{O}_v}^{\,k-2} = \bigsqcup_{\eta\in \Xi_2} \left(\eta+\varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}\right). \] Here \(\Xi_2\) is a finite set for the quotient $\varpi^{-M}\mathcal O_v^{k-2}/\varpi^N\mathcal O_v^{k-2}$. For \(y_2=\eta+y_2''\), with \(y_2''\in\varpi^N\mathcal{O}_v^{\,k-2}\), we have that \[ u\!\left(x,\binom{y_1}{\eta+y_2''},z\right) = u\!\left(x',\binom{y_1}{\eta},z'\right)\kappa(y_2''), \] where \(\kappa(y_2'')\in K_f\), the change of variables \((x,z)\mapsto(x',z')\) has Jacobian \(1\), and the character \(\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}\) is unchanged. Hence, by right \(K_f\)-invariance, integration over each coset contributes a constant multiple of the integral with \(y_2=\eta\). Consequently the \(y_2\)-integration is absorbed into a finite linear combination of right translates of \(f_{s,v}\).

Repeating the same argument for the \(y_1\)-coordinates, using the corresponding root subgroups as in the unramified case, we obtain finitely many elements \(\zeta_j\in \overline U_{2,w}(F_v)\) and constants \(c_j\) such that, for \(\Re(s)\gg0\), \[ \mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},1) = \sum_j c_j \int_{\overline U^{(0)}_{2,w}(F_v)} (\rho(\zeta_j)f_{s,v})(u)\, \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du . \] This is the ramified case for deletion of the \(y\)-coordinates in the spherical calculation.

It remains to justify the analytic continuation of the integrals above. Under the embedding of the subgroup \(\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k+2)}\) on the relevant coordinates, \(\overline U^{(0)}_{2,w}\) is an ordered product of root subgroups contained in the opposite unipotent radical of the parabolic \(P_{2,n-k+2}\). With the character \(\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}\), the integral over \(\overline U^{(0)}_{2,w}\) is one of the standard generalized Jacquet integrals attached to this degenerate principal series. Each \(\rho(\zeta_j)f_{s,v}\) is again a smooth holomorphic section of the same induced representation. Therefore the integrals converge absolutely for \(\Re(s)\gg0\) and admit meromorphic continuation in \(s\) by the standard analytic theory of local Jacquet integrals [[cite:J67]]. Since the formula is a finite sum, the same conclusion holds for \(\mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},1)\). This proves the non-Archimedean case.

We now assume that \(v\) is Archimedean. Let $D:=F_v^{k-2}$, and let \(n(r)=n_{+,\,k+1}^{\,k-2}(r)\), \(r\in D\), be the corresponding unipotent subgroup contained in \(U_k(F_v)\). By the Dixmier--Malliavin theorem, applied to the smooth right action of the Lie group \(D\), it is enough to treat sections of the form $f_{s,v}=\rho(\phi)\varphi_s$, where \(\phi\in \mathcal S(D)\), \(\varphi_s\) is a smooth holomorphic section, and \[ (\rho(\phi)\varphi_s)(g) = \int_D \phi(r)\,\varphi_s(g\,n(r))\,dr . \]

Write $Y:=\operatorname{Mat}_{2\times(k-2)}(F_v);\; Y_2:=F_v^{k-2};\; Y^{(2)}:=\left\{\binom{0}{y_2}:y_2\in Y_2\right\}\subset Y$. Choose a closed subgroup \(\overline U'_{2,w}(F_v)\subset \overline U_{2,w}(F_v)\) such that multiplication induces a diffeomorphism \[ \overline U'_{2,w}(F_v)\times u'_2(Y_2) \longrightarrow \overline U_{2,w}(F_v),\qquad (u',u'_2(y_2))\longmapsto u'u'_2(y_2), \] where $u'_2(y_2):=\overline{u\!\left(0,\binom{0}{y_2},0\right)}$.

We choose Haar measures so that \(du=du'\,dy_2\). Since \(\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}\) is trivial on \(u'_2(Y_2)\), we have $\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}\bigl(u'u'_2(y_2)\bigr) = \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u')$. For \(\Re(s)\gg0\), the integral is absolutely convergent, and the rapid decay of \(\phi\) justifies the following applications of Fubini. We have $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}_v(\rho(\phi)\varphi_s,1) &= \int_{\overline U_{2,w}(F_v)} (\rho(\phi)\varphi_s)(u)\, \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du \\ &= \int_{\overline U'_{2,w}(F_v)} \int_{Y_2} \int_D \phi(r)\, \varphi_s\!\bigl(u'u'_2(y_2)n(r)\bigr)\, dr\, \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u')\,dy_2\,du', \end{aligned}$$ where we used the fact that $u=u'u'_2(y_2)$ and $\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u'u'_2(y_2))=\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u')$. Using \[ u'u'_2(y_2)n(r) = n(r)\Bigl(n(r)^{-1}u'u'_2(y_2)n(r)\Bigr) \] and the left \(U_k(F_v)\)-invariance of \(\varphi_s\), we get \[ \varphi_s\!\bigl(u'u'_2(y_2)n(r)\bigr) = \varphi_s\!\bigl(n(r)^{-1}u'u'_2(y_2)n(r)\bigr). \] The same calculation as in the non-Archimedean case shows that conjugation by \(n(r)\) preserves the \(y_2\)-coordinate and changes the relevant \(x\)-coordinate by $\langle y_2,r\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}y_{2,i}r_i$. Thus $\psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v} \bigl(n(r)^{-1}u'u'_2(y_2)n(r)\bigr) = \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u')\, \psi_v(\langle y_2,r\rangle)$. Consequently, by a change of variables we obtain $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}_v(\rho(\phi)\varphi_s,1) &= \int_{\overline U'_{2,w}(F_v)} \int_{Y_2} \int_D \phi(r)\, \psi_v(\langle y_2,r\rangle)\, \varphi_s\!\bigl(u'u'_2(y_2)\bigr)\, dr\, \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u')\,dy_2\,du' . \end{aligned}$$

Define \[ \widehat\phi(y_2) := \int_D \phi(r)\,\psi_v(\langle y_2,r\rangle)\,dr . \] Then \(\widehat\phi\in\mathcal S(Y_2)\). Hence \[ \mathcal{F}_v(\rho(\phi)\varphi_s,1) = \int_{\overline U'_{2,w}(F_v)} \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u') \left( \int_{Y_2} \widehat\phi(y_2)\, \varphi_s\!\bigl(u'u'_2(y_2)\bigr)\,dy_2 \right) du' . \] Set \[ \varphi_{1,s}(u') := \int_{Y_2} \widehat\phi(y_2)\, \varphi_s\!\bigl(u'u'_2(y_2)\bigr)\,dy_2 . \] The rapid decay of \(\widehat\phi\) implies that \(\varphi_{1,s}\) is again obtained from \(\varphi_s\) by Schwartz convolution. In particular it is smooth, depends holomorphically on \(s\), and has uniform moderate growth on vertical strips. Thus the \(y_2\)-integration has been absorbed into the section.

Repeating the same argument for the remaining \(y_1\)-coordinates, using the corresponding root subgroups as in the unramified case, reduces the original local Fourier coefficient to an integral of the form \[ \int_{\overline U^{(0)}_{2,w}(F_v)} \varphi'_{s}(u)\, \psi^{w^{-1}}_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du , \] where \(\varphi'_s\) is obtained from the original section by finitely many Schwartz convolutions and therefore remains a smooth holomorphic family of moderate growth. As above, this is a standard generalized Jacquet integral. By [[cite:J67]], it converges absolutely for \(\Re(s)\gg0\) and admits meromorphic continuation in \(s\). Hence \(\mathcal{F}_v(f_{s,v},\cdot)\) defines a meromorphic section of \(I_{n-3,v}(s)\), as required.
nodes.role: Extends the local descent beyond normalized spherical data.
proofSketch: At a non-Archimedean place, smooth invariance and character orthogonality restrict the auxiliary coordinates to compact lattices and reduce them to finitely many translates.
At an Archimedean place, Dixmier–Malliavin factorization converts the same coordinate deletion into Fourier transforms of Schwartz functions.
In both cases, reduce to generalized Jacquet integrals and invoke their standard meromorphic continuation.
nodes.whyItMatters: It supplies the finitely many ramified local factors needed in the global descended section.

nodes.label: Lemma 4.3
nodes.title: Dixmier–Malliavin lemma
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a reductive group over an Archimedean field or a Lie group and $(\pi,V)$ a smooth representation of $G$. Then the space $V^\infty$ of smooth vectors is generated by the Schwartz algebra $\mathcal S(G)$ under convolution: for any $v\in V^\infty$ there exist $f_i\in\mathcal S(G)$ and $v_i\in V^\infty$ such that $v=\sum_i \pi(f_i)v_i$.
nodes.role: Allows Archimedean sections to be written in a form suitable for Fourier-transform coordinate deletion.
nodes.whyItMatters: It replaces compact-open invariance, which is unavailable at Archimedean places, with Schwartz convolution.

citations.title: Factorisations de fonctions et de vecteurs indéfiniment différentiables.
citations.text: Jacques Dixmier and Paul Malliavin. Factorisations de fonctions et de vecteurs indéfiniment différentiables. Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques, 102(4):307--330, 1978.

nodes.label: Jacquet's local analytic theory
nodes.title: Meromorphic continuation of generalized Jacquet integrals
nodes.statement: The proof of Proposition 4.2 invokes standard convergence in a right half-plane and meromorphic continuation for generalized local Jacquet integrals.
nodes.role: External analytic continuation input for ramified and Archimedean local integrals.
nodes.whyItMatters: The coordinate reductions alone do not extend the local integral meromorphically in $s$.

nodes.label: Proposition 4.4
nodes.title: Surjectivity and dense image of local descent
nodes.statement: Fix a local place \(v\) and \(s_0\in\mathbb C\) with \(\Re(s_0)\geq0\). Assume that, in fixed compact pictures, the continued local Fourier coefficients form a meromorphic family of continuous operators \[ \mathcal{F}_{v,s}:I_{n,v}(s)\longrightarrow I_{n-3,v}(s) \] which is holomorphic at \(s=s_0\). Then \(\mathcal{F}_{v,s_0}\) is surjective if \(v\) is non-Archimedean, and has dense image in the smooth Fréchet topology if \(v\) is Archimedean.
nodes.proofText:
Put $G=\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F_v);\; P=P_k(F_v);\; G'=\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-3)}(F_v);\; P'=P_{k-2,2(n-3)}(F_v)$, and set $a=k-2; q=n-k-1$. We first record the open-cell coordinates used in the proof. Let \(U_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}\subset U_2\) be the explicit subgroup complement representing the quotient \(U_2^w\backslash U_2\), so that $wU_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}w^{-1}=\overline U_{2,w}$ with \(\overline U_{2,w}\) as in the referenced result. Let \[ \Omega_{2q}= \begin{pmatrix} 0&J_q\\ -J_q&0 \end{pmatrix}. \] For \(Y\in\operatorname{Mat}_{2q\times a}(F_v)\) and \(Z\in\operatorname{Mat}_a(F_v)\) with \(J_aZ=Z^tJ_a\), put $Y^*=-J_aY^t\Omega_{2q},$ and $C(Y,Z) = Z-\frac12J_aY^t\Omega_{2q}Y = Z+\frac12Y^*Y$, and \[ \bar u(Y,Z)= \begin{pmatrix} I_a&0&0\\ Y&I_{2q}&0\\ C(Y,Z)&Y^*&I_a \end{pmatrix}\in\bar U'. \]

Let \(w_{P'}\) be the relative open-cell Weyl representative for \(P'\backslash G'\). Since $w_{P'}^{-1}\bar U'w_{P'}=U'$, we use the open-cell parametrization $\kappa_+(Y,Z) = \bar u(Y,Z)w_{P'} = w_{P'}u^+(Y,Z)$, where $u^+(Y,Z) = w_{P'}^{-1}\bar u(Y,Z)w_{P'}\in U'$. Thus $(Y,Z)\longmapsto P'\kappa_+(Y,Z)$ parametrizes the full open Bruhat cell of \(P'\backslash G'\). Define $\Phi_+(u,Y,Z) = P\,wu\,\iota_c\!\left(\bar u(Y,Z)w_{P'}\right),$ where $ u\in U_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}(F_v)$. Put $W=w\iota_c(w_{P'})$. A direct calculation of the relative inversion roots shows that the root coordinates contributed by \(U_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}\) and \(\iota_c(U')\) form a root-closed subgroup of the \(W\)-Bruhat cell. The remaining transverse roots are $\{e_3+e_c:4\leq c\leq k+1\}$.

Consequently \(\Phi_+\) is an algebraic isomorphism onto the subvariety $\mathcal Z_W \subset P\backslash G$ obtained by setting these transverse root coordinates equal to zero. Hence \(\mathcal Z_W\) is closed in the \(W\)-Bruhat cell and therefore locally closed in \(P\backslash G\).

It follows from the local product structure that every compactly supported smooth section on $U_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}(F_v)\times\bar U'(F_v)$, viewed as a section on \(\mathcal Z_W\) through \(\Phi_+\), extends to a compactly supported smooth section on \(P\backslash G\). At a non-Archimedean place this follows from compact-open product charts; at an Archimedean place it follows from a tubular neighborhood and a compactly supported cutoff.

We now turn to the image of the local Fourier map. Write \[ I'_v(s)=I_{n-3,v}(s) = \operatorname{Ind}_{P'}^{G'} \left( \chi_v|\det|^s \otimes1_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}(F_v)} \right), \] and realize its smooth contragredient as \[ J'_v(s) = \operatorname{Ind}_{P'}^{G'} \left( \chi_v^{-1}|\det|^{-s} \otimes1_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k-1)}(F_v)} \right). \] All inductions are normalized.

Let \(K'\subset G'\) be a maximal compact subgroup. In the fixed compact pictures, the standard pairing $[F,\xi]_s = \int_{K'}\langle F(k),\xi(k)\rangle\,dk$ is nondegenerate, \(G'\)-invariant, and independent of \(s\). It is equivalent to work with the original local model \[ \mathcal A_{v,s}(f)(g) = \int_{U_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}(F_v)} f\bigl(wu\iota_c(g)\bigr) \psi_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du, \] since it differs from the conjugated model by an invertible right translation of the source.

Let \(\xi_0\in J'_v(s_0)\) annihilate the image of \(\mathcal A_{v,s_0}\). We prove that \(\xi_0=0\). On the open cell, the compact-picture pairing takes the form \[ [F,\xi]_s = \int_{\bar U'(F_v)} \left\langle F(\kappa_+(Y,Z)), \xi(\kappa_+(Y,Z)) \right\rangle \,d\mu(Y,Z), \] where \(d\mu\) is a fixed nowhere-vanishing smooth density.

Take arbitrary $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\bar U'(F_v))$ and choose $h\in C_c^\infty(U_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}(F_v))$ such that \[ \int_{U_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}(F_v)} h(u)\psi_{\mathcal{O},v}(u)\,du=1. \] There is a compactly supported source section \(f_0\in I_{n,v}(s_0)\) satisfying $f_0(\Phi_+(u,Y,Z))=h(u)\varphi(Y,Z)$, with joint compact support in \((u,Y,Z)\).

Extend \(f_0\) and \(\xi_0\) to flat entire families \(f_s\) and \(\xi_s\) in the corresponding compact pictures. Define $B_{\mathrm{cont}}(s) = [\mathcal A_{v,s}(f_s),\xi_s]_s$ and \[ B_{\mathrm{raw}}(s) = \int_{\bar U'(F_v)} \int_{U_{2,w}^{\mathrm{c}}(F_v)} \psi_{\mathcal{O},v}(u) \left\langle f_s(\Phi_+(u,Y,Z)), \xi_s(\kappa_+(Y,Z)) \right\rangle \,du\,d\mu(Y,Z). \] The joint compact support makes \(B_{\mathrm{raw}}(s)\) entire. The operator-valued meromorphy of \(\mathcal A_{v,s}\) implies that \(B_{\mathrm{cont}}(s)\) is meromorphic and regular at \(s=s_0\).

The meromorphic identity theorem therefore gives the same equality at \(s=s_0\). Since \(\xi_0\) annihilates the image, $B_{\mathrm{cont}}(s_0)=0$. Using the prescribed restriction of \(f_0\) and the normalization of \(h\), we obtain \[ \int_{\bar U'(F_v)} \left\langle \varphi(Y,Z), \xi_0(\kappa_+(Y,Z)) \right\rangle \,d\mu(Y,Z)=0. \] Since \(\varphi\) is arbitrary, \(\xi_0\) vanishes on the full open Bruhat cell. That cell is dense and \(\xi_0\) is smooth, hence $\xi_0=0$. At a non-Archimedean place, the image is a \(G'\)-subrepresentation of the admissible finite-length representation \(I'_v(s_0)\). A proper image would give a nonzero smooth contragredient annihilator through an irreducible quotient, contradicting the preceding paragraph. Hence the map is surjective.

At an Archimedean place, if the image were not dense, Hahn--Banach would give a nonzero continuous annihilator. Convolution with \(C_c^\infty(G')\), followed by a smooth approximate identity as before, would produce a nonzero smooth contragredient annihilator, again a contradiction. Therefore the image is dense.
nodes.role: Establishes the local image property asserted in the main theorem.
proofSketch: Parametrize the open Bruhat cell of the target and embed its product with the descent unipotent into a locally closed source cell.
Assume a smooth contragredient vector annihilates the image and test it against arbitrarily prescribed compactly supported data on this cell.
Use meromorphic continuation to compare the continued pairing with the raw compactly supported integral at $s_0$.
Conclude that the annihilator vanishes on the dense open cell; finite-length duality yields surjectivity non-Archimedeanly, while Hahn–Banach and smoothing yield Archimedean density.

Outside $S$, insert the scalar from Theorem 4.1 to obtain the partial-$L$-function factor $$C^S(s)=\frac{1}{L^S(\chi^2,2s+k-1)L^S\left(\chi,s+n-\frac{k+1}{2}\right)L^S\left(\chi,s+n-\frac{k-1}{2}\right)}.$$

nodes.label: Remark 5.1
nodes.title: Application to maximal Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement:
Assume that $\chi$ is a nontrivial quadratic Hecke character, and put \[ r=n-k,\qquad a=3k-2n. \] If $r\geq1$ and $a\geq2$, then the descent may be iterated $r$ times: \[ (n,k)\longmapsto(n-3,k-2)\longmapsto\cdots\longmapsto(a,a). \] Thus the last member of the tower is the Siegel Eisenstein series on $\operatorname{Sp}_{2a}$ with the same parameter $s$. At the positive pole set $\Lambda_a$, the results of Ginzburg--Soudry (Theorem 2.2(III) [[cite:GS221]] show that the corresponding terminal residual representation has maximal partition $[2^a]$.

Combining the iterated descent with the identity of Jiang--Liu's Proposition 3.3 [[cite:JL15]] suggests adjoining a pair $3^2$ at each step and hence leads to the partition \[ [3^{2r}2^a]=[3^{2(n-k)}2^{3k-2n}]. \] Moreover, this is precisely the Richardson partition of $P_k$, by the type-$C$ induction rule [[cite:CM93|Corollary 7.3.4(ii)]]. The local wave-front bounds of [[cite:CK25]], together with [[cite:Lapid08]] and [[cite:GGS17]], therefore provide a route to showing that this partition is maximal for suitable Laurent coefficients of the original Eisenstein series.
nodes.role: Explains a prospective application of the descent tower to wave-front and Fourier-support questions.
proofSketch: Iterate $(n,k)\mapsto(n-3,k-2)$ until reaching $(a,a)$.
Import the cited maximal partition $[2^a]$ for the terminal Siegel residual representation.
Adjoin a pair $3^2$ at each reverse descent step and compare the resulting partition with the Richardson partition of $P_k$.
nodes.whyItMatters: It indicates how the descent might determine maximal Fourier coefficients of residues, while clearly stopping short of a full proof.

sourceBlocks.content: One of the most important ways to study an Eisenstein series is by analyzing its Fourier coefficients parameterized by certain unipotent orbits. In this paper, we give a detailed analysis of such coefficients in a new situation, that of a degenerate Eisenstein series on the symplectic group.

Let $F$ be a number field and $\mathbb{A}$ its ring of adeles. For any positive integer $k$, $3\leqslant k <n$, we define $P_{k}:=P_{k,n} = M_{k}\ltimes U_{k}$ to be the standard maximal parabolic subgroup of the symplectic group $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}$, with the Levi subgroup $M_k \cong \operatorname{GL}_k\times \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)}$. Denote by $\chi$ a Hecke character. Then for this Levi subgroup, consider the representation $\chi|\det|^s\otimes \operatorname{{\bf 1}}_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)}}$ on $\operatorname{GL}_k(\mathbb{A})\times \operatorname{Sp}_{2(n-k)}(\mathbb{A})$. Letting $U_k(\mathbb{A})$ act trivially, we parabolically induce this representation to $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(\mathbb{A})$, and denote the resulting representation by $I_n(s)$, whose precise definition can be found in (the referenced result) in Section 2.3.
Let $f_s$ be a holomorphic section in $I_n(s)$, and form the degenerate Eisenstein series of $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(\mathbb{A})$ defined for $\Re(s)\gg0$, by
$$ E_{f_s}(g) = \sum_{\gamma\in P_k(F)\setminus \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(F)}f_s(\gamma g). $$

Then $E_{f_s}$ is a meromorphic function of $s$ and may be continued to the whole plane. This Eisenstein series has a certain nonzero Fourier coefficient attached to the unipotent radical $U_2$ of the standard maximal parabolic subgroup $P_2$. For $P_1$, such a coefficient vanishes (for details, see [[cite:GIN06]], Chapter 5). Let $\psi_\mathcal{O}$ be the generic character attached to the unipotent radical $U_2(\mathbb{A})$, whose precise definition can be found in \hyperref[sec204]{Section 2.4}. We define
